title: When does the shortcut pay?
hook: Straight along a parallel versus the shortest route: how big is the gap?

knows: great circles are shorter than constant-heading routes
doesNotKnow: when the difference starts to matter

misconception: The great-circle saving is large even on a short east-west trip.
objective: The learner can say that the great-circle saving is tiny over short east-west distances and grows quickly with distance and with latitude.

claims.text: Two places 1,000 km apart along 40 N: the great circle is about 0.7 km shorter than the parallel.
claims.source: Sphere R = 6,371.0088 km. Points at +/- (d / (R cos lat)) / 2 of longitude about 10 E; great-circle length d3-geo geoDistance x R. Node (builder's scratch script; nothing precomputed ships, all values are computed at runtime from the same formula): 1,000 km spans 11.7 degrees of longitude, great circle 999.28 km, saving 0.72 km (0.07%). The stage readout uses the same function.

claims.text: At 5,000 km along 40 N the saving is 96 km: five times the distance, over 130 times the saving.
claims.source: Node: 95.61 km at 5,000 km (1.91%), 0.72 km at 1,000 km; ratio 132.6. Other values computed for the stage: 2,000 km 5.83 km; 8,000 km 428 km (5.35%). The brief's figures of 1.95% (5,000 km) and 5.7% (8,000 km) are not what d3-geo gives; the stage shows the computed ones.

claims.text: At 60 N the same 5,000 km saves 398 km.
claims.source: Node: 398.31 km (7.97%) at 60 N; 18.09 km (0.36%) at 20 N. At 60 N and 8,000 km the great circle peaks at 79.9 N, inside the map.

claims.text: Following a parallel is a constant due-east heading (a rhumb line of bearing 90 degrees).
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, ch. 7 (cited from memory): a parallel is a loxodrome of bearing 90 degrees. Used for the stage caption 'Red: due east along the parallel'.

claims.text: On the globe the parallel bends away from the shortest path more the longer it is and the nearer the pole, so short hops gain almost nothing.
claims.source: Follows from the node table: at 5,000 km the saving is 18 km at 20 N, 96 km at 40 N, 398 km at 60 N; at 40 N it is 0.72 km at 1,000 km and 95.6 km at 5,000 km. Not a claim about flights.

claims.text: Sphere model, not a flight time. A Mercator map stretches the north, so the shortest route (blue) looks longer than the parallel (red) but is shorter.
claims.source: Model label: sphere of R = 6,371.0088 km (IUGG mean radius); no winds, airspace or fuel stops are modelled and the lesson makes no flight claim.

recall.question: Why does a great-circle route save almost nothing on a 1,000 km east-west trip at 40 N?
options: At that distance the parallel is almost the same line as the shortest route
Great circles are not really shorter
The Earth is flat over short distances in every direction, so there is never a saving
recall.why: The saving grows much faster than distance (0.7 km at 1,000 km, 96 km at 5,000 km), so over a short hop the two routes nearly coincide.
